463.title: Here am I (Isaiah 6:1–8)
463.hook: Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, and says here am I, send me
463.howItsDone: Christians sing the seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' in the Sanctus of the communion service, and Isaiah 6 is often read at ordinations and when people are commissioned for mission or service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, we began the prophets with the word prophet, and your line was truth to power. Did you hear an uncomfortable truth without arguing back? Day four hundred sixty-three.

It begins with a date: "In the year that king Uzziah died." A king is dead, and a whole kingdom is waiting to see what comes next. In that year, a man named Isaiah is in the Temple in Jerusalem, and he sees something. The Lord, sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and the hem of his robe filling the whole Temple. Above him, beings with six wings each, calling to one another. The doorposts shake. The house fills with smoke. Today, the moment Isaiah is called, and the two words he answers with.
screen: `THE YEAR KING UZZIAH DIED.` → `A THRONE, HIGH AND LIFTED UP.` → `THE DOORPOSTS SHAKE.`

segments.voice: The text calls these beings seraphim, a name some readers link to a Hebrew word for burning. They cover their faces with two wings, their feet with two, and fly with two, and they call: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Churches still sing that line in the Sanctus at communion, and in hymns. And here is Isaiah's first reaction. Not wonder. Terror. "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips." He doesn't say he's done terrible things. He says his mouth is unclean, the very thing a prophet needs. Then one of the seraphim flies to the altar, takes a live coal with tongs, and touches it to his lips. Your guilt is taken away, it says. And now, at last, a question from the throne. Notice it isn't a command. "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" And Isaiah: "Here am I; send me." In Hebrew that's hineni, one short word: here I am. It's what Abraham says when God calls him, what Moses says at the burning bush, what the boy Samuel says in the night. It doesn't mean I'm qualified. Isaiah has just said he isn't. It means I'm present, I'm listening, I'm available. And it comes before he knows the job. The next verses give him a hard message for a people who won't listen. He says yes first. Christians hear their own calls in this scene at ordinations and at sendings for mission, and in ordinary moments too: someone asks who will go, and a hand goes up.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `WOE IS ME: UNCLEAN LIPS.` · `A LIVE COAL ON THE MOUTH.` · `HINENI: HERE I AM.` · then, large: `HERE AM I; SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say here am I. Settle, and breathe. Notice where you are right now: the chair, the room, the sounds, the light. Let yourself be fully here, the way the word hineni means. Then think of one place this week where someone is asking, in their own way, who will go: a neighbor, a coworker, a family member, a cause. You don't have to fix it. Just turn toward it. If you pray, you can say Isaiah's words: here am I; send me. If you don't, simply say here I am, and mean it. The bell holds the time.
Here am I. Hineni in Hebrew: present and available, the answer of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah, said before knowing the job.
Your line: send me. Today, when someone asks for a volunteer, a hand, or just a listener, try saying it out loud: here I am. Day four hundred sixty-three.

what a scholar hears: hineni, a single word of readiness. the seraphim's threefold holy lives on in the Sanctus, and the call is dated by a king's death, not by a calendar year.

464.title: Swords into ploughshares (Isaiah 2:2–4)
464.hook: the nations will beat swords into ploughshares and learn war no more
464.howItsDone: Isaiah 2:4 is often read in Advent and at services of prayer for peace; the phrase study war no more comes from the African American spiritual Down by the Riverside, sung in churches and at peace gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah in the Temple, here am I, and your line was send me. Where did you raise your hand? Day four hundred sixty-four.

In the garden of the United Nations in New York there's a bronze statue of a muscular man. He holds a hammer high over his head. In his other hand is a sword, and he's bending its blade. The end of the sword is already curling into the shape of a plow. The statue was a gift from the Soviet Union, during the Cold War, while both sides were building bombs. Its title comes from an old Hebrew prophet, writing in a small kingdom squeezed between empires. Today, the line that sculptor was reaching for.
screen: `A STATUE AT THE UNITED NATIONS.` → `A HAMMER OVER A SWORD.` → `THE BLADE BECOMING A PLOW.`

segments.voice: Isaiah, chapter two, sees a day to come: the mountain of the Lord's house raised above the hills, and all nations streaming to it. Not dragged. Streaming, like a river running uphill. They come saying, let's go up, so he'll teach us his ways. And then, in the King James Bible: "and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Take it literally. A plowshare is the iron blade that cuts the soil. A pruning hook trims vines. Iron was precious; you didn't throw it away. You reforged it. The same metal that killed now feeds. Weapons aren't buried or hidden. They're turned into farming tools. And notice the last phrase: they shall not learn war any more. War here is something learned, taught, practiced, studied. Which means it can be unlearned. The same vision appears almost word for word in the prophet Micah, who adds that everyone will sit under their own vine and fig tree, with no one to make them afraid. And one more thing: the prophet Joel turns the image around, calling people to beat their plowshares into swords for battle. The Bible knows both directions. Isaiah's points to the end of the story. Christians often read it as a promise of God's kingdom, and hear Jesus' blessing on the peacemakers as a call to live toward it now. Some, Mennonites and Quakers among them, take it as a call to refuse war entirely. Others hold it as the goal while believing defense can be just. And an old African American spiritual, Down by the Riverside, carries the last phrase into song: study war no more.
screen: `ALL NATIONS STREAMING TO THE MOUNTAIN.` · `THE SAME IRON, REFORGED.` · `WAR IS LEARNED, SO IT CAN BE UNLEARNED.` · `JOEL TURNS IT AROUND.` · then, large: `NEITHER SHALL THEY LEARN WAR ANY MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one sword you could reforge. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small weapon you carry: a sharp tone you use with someone, a grudge you sharpen, a habit of winning arguments, a post you keep meaning to write. Hold it in your mind like a piece of iron. Then picture the hammer, and the blade slowly becoming a tool. What would that same energy look like if it built something? A conversation instead of a jab. Help instead of a grudge. If you pray, you can pray for peace in one place you know of, by name. The bell holds the time.
Swords into ploughshares. Isaiah's picture of peace: the iron of war reforged into tools that feed people, and war itself unlearned.
Your line: study war no more. Today, do one peaceful act on purpose: end a quarrel, skip a jab, or turn the energy of an argument into something useful. Day four hundred sixty-four.

465.title: Unto us a child (Isaiah 9:2–7)
465.hook: the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light
465.howItsDone: Isaiah 9:2–7 is one of the most common readings at Christmas services, including the traditional service of lessons and carols, and many Christians light candles through Advent while waiting for Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, swords into ploughshares, and your line was study war no more. What peaceful act did you choose? Day four hundred sixty-five.

In December, in concert halls and churches in many countries, a choir waits for a particular chorus. The violins start running, light and quick. Then the voices come in, one part after another, tossing the same words back and forth. And then the whole choir lands, all together, on a string of names, hammered out one at a time. Handel wrote it in London, and it was first heard in Dublin in 1742. But the words weren't his. They come from the prophet Isaiah, written more than seven centuries before Jesus, to a kingdom with an army on its border. Today, the people who walked in darkness.
screen: `A CHOIR STANDS IN DECEMBER.` → `A STRING OF NAMES, HAMMERED OUT.` → `THE WORDS ARE ISAIAH'S.`

segments.voice: Isaiah's world was dark in a literal way. The Assyrian empire was on the march, and the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up around the Sea of Galilee, were among the first to be overrun. Into that, Isaiah says, in the King James Bible: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined." Notice the tense. Have seen. The prophet speaks of the rescue as if it's already happened. Then he names the light: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace." Not a general. Not a weapon. A baby. The boots of the soldiers, Isaiah says, will be burned as fuel for the fire. And this child's peace will have no end, on the throne of David. Who is the child? Here readers differ, and it's worth saying plainly. Many Jewish readers have understood it as a royal child of Isaiah's own time, often King Hezekiah, or as a future king of David's line. Christians, from the Gospels on, read it as Jesus. Matthew's Gospel quotes this very passage when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the first place the darkness fell. For Christians, the light rose exactly where the shadow had begun. That's why these words come back every Christmas: a child, given, into a dark place.
screen: `ASSYRIA, AND A DARK NORTH.` · `HAVE SEEN: SPOKEN AS IF DONE.` · `NOT A GENERAL. A CHILD.` · `GALILEE, WHERE THE SHADOW FELL.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE THAT WALKED IN DARKNESS HAVE SEEN A GREAT LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle, or picture one. If you can, light a real one and set it in front of you. If not, imagine it clearly. Settle, and breathe. Look at the flame. Notice how small it is, and how much of the room it changes. Then think of one dark place you know about right now: a family going through something, a city in the news, a corner of your own life. Hold the flame and that place together in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for that place by name. The bell holds the time.
Unto us a child. Isaiah's promise of a child born for a people in darkness, which Christians read as the birth of Jesus.
Your line: a great light. Today, be a small one: bring one bit of light into a place that feels dark for someone, a call, a kind word, a visit. Day four hundred sixty-five.

466.title: The wolf and the lamb (Isaiah 11:1–9)
466.hook: a shoot from a stump, and a little child will lead them
466.howItsDone: Isaiah 11 is often read during Advent, and some families and congregations make a Jesse tree, hanging ornaments for the stories of Jesus's ancestors; the Quaker painter Edward Hicks painted this vision as The Peaceable Kingdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unto us a child, and your line was a great light. Where did you bring a little light? Day four hundred sixty-six.

A forest a few years after the loggers have gone: stumps everywhere. Flat, gray, finished. But look closer at some of them. Out of the side of an old stump, a thin green shoot, with two or three leaves. The tree was cut down. The roots weren't. Isaiah had watched the royal family of David shrink and fail. Kings who trusted armies instead of God. A kingdom being cut down to the ground. And from that stump, he saw something growing. Today, the shoot, and the strange, gentle world it brings.
screen: `A FOREST OF STUMPS.` → `A GREEN SHOOT FROM THE SIDE.` → `DAVID'S LINE, CUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." Jesse was David's father. Some readers hear in that a return past David, to the roots, before the kings went wrong. On this new shoot, Isaiah says, the spirit of the Lord will rest: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, the fear of the Lord. This king won't judge by what his eyes see or his ears hear. He'll judge the poor with fairness. And then the picture everyone remembers: "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them." Every pair is a predator and its dinner. The wolf and the lamb. The leopard and the young goat. A baby playing at the hole of a snake. The world's whole food chain, the logic of eat or be eaten, stops. And who's in charge of this new world? Not a lion. A little child, leading. One slip worth catching: people sometimes quote it as the lion shall lie down with the lamb. The text never says that. It's the wolf that dwells with the lamb, the leopard that lies down with the kid. The vision ends: "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain." Christians read the shoot of Jesse as Jesus, and some churches hang a Jesse tree in Advent, tracing his family. Jewish tradition reads it as the hope of a messiah still to come. Both keep the picture of a world where nothing preys on anything.
screen: `A ROD OUT OF THE STEM OF JESSE.` · `A KING WHO JUDGES THE POOR FAIRLY.` · `PREDATOR AND PREY, TOGETHER.` · `NOT THE LION: THE WOLF.` · then, large: `A LITTLE CHILD SHALL LEAD THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for new growth from old wood. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that feels cut down: a friendship that ended, a plan that failed, a part of you that went quiet. Picture it as a stump. Then look closely, the way you would in a forest. Is there a small green shoot anywhere? A new habit, a reconnection, a lesson, a beginning you hadn't noticed. Let your attention rest on it, without demanding it be a tree yet. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
The wolf and the lamb. Isaiah's picture of a peace so deep that predator and prey live together, and a little child leads them.
screen: `THE WOLF AND THE LAMB — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a little child shall lead. Today, let a child, or the most overlooked person in the room, lead you once: follow their question, their game, their idea. Day four hundred sixty-six.

467.title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40:1–11)
467.hook: speak tenderly; every valley lifted; he gathers the lambs in his arms
467.howItsDone: Christians read Isaiah 40 in Advent, often alongside the story of John the Baptist, and Handel's Messiah opens with it; in Jewish practice it is the prophetic reading on Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wolf and the lamb, and your line was a little child shall lead. Who led you yesterday? Day four hundred sixty-seven.

Read Isaiah straight through and something happens at chapter forty. Chapter after chapter, the book has been full of warnings, judgments and armies. Assyria is coming. Jerusalem is in danger. The prophet's voice is often hard. The chapter just before ends with a warning that the king's treasures, and his sons, will one day be carried off to Babylon. Then you turn the page, and the voice changes, as if a different season has arrived. Now it speaks to a city whose hard service is over, and to a people who need a road home. And the very first word God speaks to them in this new section isn't a rebuke, or an explanation, or a lesson about what went wrong. Today, that first word.
screen: `CHAPTER AFTER CHAPTER OF WARNING.` → `TURN THE PAGE.` → `CARRIED OFF TO BABYLON.` → `THE FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." Said twice, the way you'd say it to someone crying: it's okay, it's okay. In Hebrew it's nachamu, nachamu ammi. Then: "Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem." The Hebrew there is lovely: literally, speak to the heart of Jerusalem. It's the phrase used elsewhere in the Bible for someone wooing, or reassuring, someone they love. Tell her, God says, that her hard service is over. Then a voice cries out: make a road through the wilderness for God. "Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain." Picture road builders filling every dip and leveling every hill, so God can come straight to his people and bring them home. Then a reminder that people are like grass; the grass withers, but God's word stands. And it ends with a picture so tender it's almost surprising: "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young." Not driving the flock. Carrying the smallest ones, and walking slowly for the mothers. Some scholars think this chapter begins a new part of the book, written later for the exiles; others hold the whole book to be Isaiah's. Christians hear the voice in the wilderness as John the Baptist, as all four Gospels say. And Jewish communities read this chapter on the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the Temple: they call it the Sabbath of comfort.
screen: `COMFORT YE, COMFORT YE.` · `SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.` · `EVERY VALLEY EXALTED.` · `HE CARRIES THE LAMBS.` · then, large: `COMFORT YE MY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak tenderly to someone, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's in a hard season: worn out, far from home, grieving, or just tired of being told what they did wrong. Notice the urge to fix them or explain things. Set it down. Instead, imagine speaking to their heart, the way this chapter does. What would you say first? Keep it short and kind. Say it silently, twice, the way the prophet does. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Comfort ye. Nachamu in Hebrew: the first word of a new section of Isaiah, spoken twice, speaking tenderly to the heart.
Your line: comfort ye my people. Today, send one tender message to someone in a hard season. No advice, no fixing. Just comfort, first. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

468.title: Wings like eagles (Isaiah 40:28–31)
468.hook: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength
468.howItsDone: Christians often memorize Isaiah 40:31, and it is frequently read at funerals and shared with people facing illness or exhaustion; it also appears in many hymns and worship songs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word to the exiles, and your line was comfort ye my people. Who did you speak tenderly to? Day four hundred sixty-eight.

It's mile twenty of a marathon. The crowds have thinned out. The legs that felt so light at the start now feel like wet sand. Runners call it the wall, and even the young, fit ones hit it. Now stretch that wall across years instead of miles. That's where the people Isaiah speaks to are: worn down by a long, long wait for something to change. Some are saying out loud that God has forgotten them, that their cause has slipped past his notice. The same chapter that opened with comfort ends by answering them. Today, the answer for people who are tired.
screen: `MILE TWENTY. THE WALL.` → `A LONG, LONG WAIT.` → `HAS GOD FORGOTTEN US?`

segments.voice: First the prophet asks, almost impatient: "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?" The one who made everything doesn't run out. And then the turn: he gives power to the faint. Even young people, Isaiah says, get tired; even strong young men stumble and fall. Strength isn't a matter of being young or fit. And then the line people have stitched onto pillows and painted on locker-room walls: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Two things to notice. First, wait. The Hebrew word leans toward hope; some translations even render it those who hope in the Lord. It isn't sitting idle. It's leaning toward God, the way you lean toward a door when you hear the car pull in. Second, renew. The Hebrew verb can also mean to change or exchange, and some readers hear a trade: spent strength for new. And here is a detail that surprises people: look at the order. Fly, then run, then walk. It goes down, not up. You might expect the big finish to be soaring. Instead it ends with walking and not fainting. Some readers call that the honest part. Some days soar. Some days run. And plenty of days, the gift is to walk and not faint. That may be why people carry this verse into hospital rooms and funerals: it doesn't promise flying every day.
screen: `THE CREATOR FAINTETH NOT.` · `WAIT: LEANING TOWARD GOD.` · `RENEW: A TRADE OF STRENGTH.` · `FLY, RUN, WALK: IT GOES DOWN.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS AS EAGLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest before you run. Settle, and let your body be heavy. Let your shoulders drop, your hands go loose, your feet rest flat. Notice where you're tired: your eyes, your back, your heart. Don't push past it. Just admit it. Then, for the rest of the sit, simply wait, leaning toward God or toward stillness, expecting nothing in particular. Breathe out the spent strength. Breathe in, as if trading it for new. If you pray, you can say the line slowly: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength. The bell holds the time.
Wings like eagles. Isaiah's promise to the tired: those who wait on God exchange their strength, and soar, and run, and keep walking.
Your line: wings like eagles. Today, before the next demanding thing, stop for one minute and rest on purpose. Then go, walking, if not flying. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

469.title: Called by name (Isaiah 43:1–3)
469.hook: fear not, I have called you by name; when you pass through the waters
469.howItsDone: Isaiah 43:1–3 is often read at Christian baptisms and confirmations, and Christians turn to it in times of fear or illness; it is also set in hymns and songs used in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a promise for the tired, and your line was wings like eagles. Did you rest before you ran? Day four hundred sixty-nine.

A crowded airport. Hundreds of people, announcements in three languages, nobody looking at anybody. Then, over the noise, someone calls out your name. Not "excuse me." Not "sir" or "ma'am." Your name. And you turn, instantly, before you've even thought about it. A name cuts through. The exiles Isaiah speaks to were a small, defeated people inside a great empire, easy to lose in the crowd: unseen, overlooked, swallowed. Isaiah has comforted them and promised them strength. Now he says something even more personal. Today, the name.

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Notice the verbs. Created, formed. Formed is a potter's word, the same one used when God shapes the first human from the dust in Genesis. Then redeemed: the word for a family member who buys back a relative sold into debt, or buys back the family land. Then called by name. Then the three words of today's carry: thou art mine. Not a possession, the way you own a phone. Belonging, the way a child belongs to a family. And then the promise, with water and fire: "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned." It doesn't say you'll never pass through the waters. It says when. The flood and the fire are assumed. What's promised is company in them, and that they won't sweep you away. These words were first spoken to a whole people, Jacob and Israel, and Jewish readers hear them that way. Christians also hear them personally, and some churches read them at baptisms, where someone is named and passes through the water. This week in the prophets: here am I, swords into plowshares, unto us a child, the wolf and the lamb, comfort ye, wings like eagles, and today, called by name. A week that moved from a prophet saying send me to God saying you are mine.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say your name as if God said it. Settle, and breathe. Say your own name silently, the one people who love you use. Notice how it feels: maybe tender, maybe awkward, maybe heavy with what other people have said in that tone. Now say it again, slowly, as if it were spoken by someone who made you and isn't disappointed. Then let the next words follow: fear not. Let them rest on whatever you're passing through right now. If you pray, you can simply listen. The bell holds the time.
Called by name. God's word to the exiles in Isaiah forty-three: created, formed, redeemed, and named. Fear not; you are mine.
Your line: you are mine. Today, use people's names on purpose: the cashier, the coworker, the neighbor. Let someone feel seen in the crowd. Day four hundred sixty-nine.
